newsitem.title: USA: U.S. to sell $29 bln of securities next week.
newsitem.headline: U.S. to sell $29 bln of securities next week.

text.p: The Treasury Department on Wednesday announced a $29 billion quarterly refunding to be held next week and unveiled a series of steps to make U.S. Savings Bonds more attractive to individual investors.
Treasury said next week's auctions will refund $27.4 billion of maturing securities and raise $1.6 billion of new cash.
The auctions will consist of $17 billion of three-year notes to be sold next Tuesday and $12 billion of 10-year notes to be sold next Wednesday.
As reported on Monday, Treasury expects to pay down $65 billion of government debt during the second quarter. The record paydown reflects a surge in tax receipts, primarily from individuals.
"This ... suggests that the (budget) deficit could be down for the fifth year in a row," Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin told a news conference.
In light of that, the Treasury's private-sector Borrowing Advisory Committee recommended that the department drop two of the current six auctions of 10-year notes that it holds each year.

"We have no decision yet," Deputy Assistant Treasury Secretary Roger Anderson told reporters when asked about scrapping some note sales. But he added, "We will have to consider our auction schedule as we go forward."
There is no timetable for making a decision, he added.
Despite the improved outlook for the budget deficit, Rubin said that the U.S. savings rate was "far too low" and needed to be raised.
To help bring that about, Rubin said that Treasury was taking steps to boost the return for investors who buy U.S Savings Bonds.
The changes, to take effect on Thursday, include paying interest on the bonds monthly instead of every six months and changing the way in which interest rates are calculated.

Rather than using a combination of short- and long-term market interest rates to set the yield on the bonds, Treasury will use only long-term rates. It will also raise the percentage of market rates that will be paid on the bonds to 90 percent from 85 percent.
The moves will raise the yield on Savings Bond holdings by about 1 percentage point in the first five years of ownership and by about one quarter percentage point for later years.

Treasury also proposed changes in the way it runs its bill auctions. It plans to require three-decimal-point bidding at all its regular bill sales and to lower the reporting threshold for investors who have net long positions at the auctions to $1 billion from $2 billion.
Treasury will publish the proposals for public comment next week.

After next week's refunding auctions, Treasury will need to pay down $18.3 billion in market borrowings during the rest of the second quarter. That can be done through regular sales of three- and six-month and one-year bills, and two- and five-year notes in May and June.
"Cash management bills may be needed to cover the low points in the cash balance in early June," Anderson said.
As previously reported, the Treasury estimates its net market borrowing requirement in the July-September third quarter will be $40-$45 billion, assuming a $40-billion cash balance on September 30.
